**Section.** The whole piece: applies.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.**
- **The purpose is clear at once.** The title "Planning a vegetable bed" (about x 160–750, y 60–110) is the first thing you see. Below it are three plain, task-named headings: "Preparing the soil", "Choosing what to plant" and "Watering". A first-time viewer can say "a short beginner's guide to starting a vegetable bed" within a second. Each heading names what its paragraph holds, so the page can be scanned without reading the body. Keep the headings literal and task-shaped if more sections are added.
- **Nothing is there without a reason, and it all reads as one piece.** There are no rules, boxes, icons or decorations. There is one typeface, one heading colour and one body colour. All four headings are styled and spaced the same way, and every block shares one left edge at x≈160. The copy is concrete and finished: it says "six hours of sun", "the depth of a spade", "radishes, lettuce, and bush beans", and "twice a week, rather than a little every day". It speaks to the reader, with no filler and no placeholder text. That restraint suits a short how-to and should stay.

**Couldn't judge from a still.** I couldn't run the crop script because Bash was denied here. The image is 1280×800, about one screen, so I worked from the whole image at full size, and this doesn't change any answer.

**Checklist.** The whole piece: 8 lines, 8 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure.

sections.report:
**Walk (working notes)**

First read: the eye lands on "Planning a vegetable bed" (large, bold, blue, top left). It then drops through the three blue subheads in order. It reads as a short how-to article for beginner gardeners, and it feels calm and plain. The image is 1280×800, one screen, so I worked from the whole image.

Job (assumed): a simple instructional web page for a beginner gardener.

What matters first:
- One element stands clearly above the rest: **yes**. The title is about 50 px, bold and blue, and is the largest thing on the page.
- Each text level is distinct, with no near-duplicate sizes: **yes**. I see three sizes with big steps between them: title about 50 px, headings about 30 px, body about 18 px. There are no captions.
- Headings differ from body text in more than size: **yes**. They are bold and blue, and the body is regular and near-black.

No line was answered no or unsure, so there were no reference entries to open.

**Section.** What matters first (hierarchy): applies.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.**
- **A clean three-step scale.** The sizes are roughly 50, 30 and 18 px, so each level has an obvious job and no two sizes are close. The title is clearly the place to start, and the eye drops straight from it to the subheads in reading order.
- **Headings marked twice.** The subheads (y≈242, 368, 494) differ from the body by weight and colour as well as size. That makes the three steps easy to scan and find again, which suits a how-to page that a reader returns to while working.

**Checklist.** What matters first: 3 lines, 3 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

**Section.** Arrangement and space: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Does the visual weight balance, with no side, crowded or empty, that makes the page look about to tip? / Do the main divisions of the frame follow one proportion, rather than arbitrary splits?** The text column runs from x≈160 to x≈945 in a 1280 px frame. That leaves about 160 px on the left and about 335 px on the right, a 160 / 785 / 335 split with no clear ratio. All the content ends by y≈545, so the bottom third (about 255 px) is empty too. The column is too far from the left edge to read as a deliberate left-set column, and too far off-centre to read as centred. So the page leans a little toward the upper left, as if a centred container slipped. Arnheim (*Art and Visual Perception*, "Balance") says a heavy side needs a counterweight or a clear reason to be heavy. To fix it, pick one: centre the column (about 247 px each side), or keep it left-set and make the right space clearly deliberate, for example a margin column that could hold notes or a small image. The empty bottom comes from the short content and is fine. Taste. Weight: minor.

**What's working.** Grouping by space is clean. Each blue heading sits about 10 px above its paragraph and about 30 px below the paragraph before it, so each heading belongs to its own step and the four steps read as four separate blocks without rules or boxes. Every block also hangs from one left edge at x≈160, so the eye runs straight down the headings.

**Checklist.** Arrangement and space: 13 lines, 11 yes, 2 no (visual weight balances; main divisions follow one proportion), 0 unsure

**Section.** Text: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Do paragraph lines run about 45 to 75 characters?** The body paragraphs run from about x 160 to x 945, roughly 85 to 92 characters per line. For example, "Dig to the depth of a spade and mix in compost from last year's heap. Rake the surface level" is one line. With no sidebar or image beside it, the column is wider than comfortable, and on each line break the eye has a longer trip back to the left edge. Every paragraph here is only one or two lines, so in this capture the cost is small. It will grow if the article gets longer. Bringhurst, *The Elements of Typographic Style* §2.1.2, gives 45 to 75 characters, with 66 as the ideal. The fix is to narrow the text column (and the headings with it) to about 65 characters, which is around 600 px at this size. The large empty band on the right shows there is no other content competing for the width. Convention. Weight: minor.
2. **Are quotation marks curly, and are dashes and ellipses the true characters?** The apostrophe in "last year's" (around x 660, y 282) is a straight typewriter mark, not a curly one. At body size the reader barely sees it, but it shows the text was not set with care. Use the true apostrophe (’) and check any other quotes on the page. No checked source supports the curly-quote point, so this is common sense, not a cited rule. Taste. Weight: minor.

**What's working.**
- Body text is a plain sans at a comfortable size (around 17 px), near-black on white, with generous line spacing of about 1.6. That makes it easy to read on screen, and the extra spacing partly makes up for the long lines.
- The bold title is spaced tightly and kerned evenly. It holds together as one solid shape and is clearly the display level above the subheads.

**Checklist.** Text: 30 lines, 28 yes, 2 no (lines of 45 to 75 characters; curly quotes and true dashes)

**Section.** Color: applies.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.**
- There's only one hue. A single mid-dark blue (about #1A5FAA by eye) is used only on the title (y≈60–110) and the three subheads (y≈228, 352, 478), and the body is near-black on white. All the color goes on the structure, so you can scan down the left edge and find each step. Nothing else on the page competes for that color.
- The value range holds up in grayscale. The blue is dark enough to stay clearly darker than white, and the headings also stand out by size and weight. In grayscale the hierarchy would look the same. Color adds to the structure but the structure doesn't depend on it.

**Couldn't judge from a still.** Whether the blue headings are links. Blue text on a web page usually means a link, so if these headings can't be clicked, readers may try. That belongs to the interface section, not to color.

**Checklist.** Color: 9 lines, 9 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure.

**Section.** Pictures: skipped. The page has no photos, illustrations, icons, logos or marks. It is only a heading, subheadings and body text on white, and nothing looks like an empty slot or a broken image.

**Findings**
None.

**Checklist.** Pictures: skipped
